description: A period-piece fairy tale: Taylor plays a modern-day Juliet in a Regency gown, all castle balconies, ballroom dances, and a happy ending Shakespeare never wrote.

pops.text: She wrote the song in about 20 minutes on her bedroom floor — and later called it one of the easiest songs she ever wrote.
That castle isn't in Europe. It's Castle Gwynn in Arrington, Tennessee, home of the Tennessee Renaissance Festival.
Director Trey Fanjoy shot the entire video in just two days in August 2008.
The male lead is Justin Gaston, a model and Nashville Star contestant — Taylor picked him on a friend's recommendation.
Taylor learned the ballroom dance choreography about 15 minutes before filming it.
The video flips Shakespeare's ending: instead of tragedy, Romeo shows up with a ring and proposes.
The balcony gown was custom-designed with Taylor's own input, inspired by Regency-era fashion.
The video won Video of the Year and Female Video of the Year at the 2009 CMT Music Awards.
In 2021 she re-recorded it as "Love Story (Taylor's Version)" to reclaim her masters — fans say her grown-up voice hits the high notes even harder.

title: Love Story

description: Taylor plays both the curly-haired girl next door and her brunette cheerleader rival, pining for the boy next door through notes held up in bedroom windows.

pops.text: Taylor plays BOTH girls — the nerdy protagonist with big glasses and the "horrible, scary, intimidating" popular cheerleader.
The love interest is Lucas Till, whom Taylor met on the set of Hannah Montana: The Movie.
Filmed over two days in Gallatin and Hendersonville, Tennessee — the prom scenes used a real high school's students as extras.
The window-sign conversations were a set trick — the "houses" weren't actually next door to each other.
She used a body double for every shot where both characters appear together.
The two prom dresses were sourced from Jovani Fashion.
Director Roman White scrapped her planned choreography for the bedroom dance, replacing it with what Taylor called "the dumbest moves".
This video won Best Female Video at the 2009 VMAs — beating Beyoncé's "Single Ladies".
Which led to the most infamous VMA moment ever: Kanye West storming the stage mid-acceptance speech.

title: You Belong with Me

description: A joyful parade of dance personas — ballerina, hip-hop crew, cheerleader — as Taylor shrugs off her critics with deliberately goofy moves.

pops.text: This was the lead single from 1989, her first official full-pop album after four country records.
It debuted at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — her second chart-topper.
The video was directed by Mark Romanek, the man behind Johnny Cash's "Hurt".
Taylor plays a ballerina, a hip-hop dancer, a cheerleader, and more — dancing badly on purpose in several scenes.
The "players gonna play" lyric was her direct answer to years of tabloid criticism about her dating life.
It became one of the best-selling digital singles of all time.
The dancers were real professionals from each style — Taylor was the only amateur on set, by design.
"Shake It Off" earned three Grammy nominations, including Record and Song of the Year.
She later said the song was about learning to laugh at the noise instead of fighting it.

title: Shake It Off

description: A satirical fever dream in a Long Island mansion, where Taylor gleefully plays the unhinged "psycho ex-girlfriend" the tabloids accused her of being.

pops.text: The whole song is satire — Taylor playing the "crazy serial dater" the media painted her as.
Shot over three days at Oheka Castle in Huntington, New York — the second-largest private home in America.
Director Joseph Kahn took visual cues from Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange: all symmetry and barely-contained madness.
Her ill-fated boyfriend is played by model Sean O'Pry.
The golf-club-to-the-car scene is a direct nod to the Tiger Woods scandal headlines.
She stabs a cake, drops his phone in a fountain, and cuts holes in his shirts — all in couture.
It knocked her own "Shake It Off" off #1 — she became the first woman in Billboard history to replace herself at the top.
Seven weeks at #1 made it her longest-running chart-topper at the time.
The video ends with a new, nearly identical boyfriend pulling up — the cycle starts all over.

title: Blank Space

description: A blockbuster-style action short: Taylor leads an army of celebrity alter-egos into battle against Selena Gomez's villain Arsyn.

pops.text: The single version adds a brand-new Kendrick Lamar verse — the video premiered at the 2015 Billboard Music Awards.
Selena Gomez plays the villain Arsyn; the squad includes Lena Dunham, Hailee Steinfeld, Zendaya, and more.
Joseph Kahn directed it as a full sci-fi action short, complete with a training montage.
Every star got a character name and poster — it was marketed like a summer blockbuster.
The song is widely believed to be about her feud with Katy Perry — the two later reconciled.
It debuted at #1 on the Hot 100 with one of the biggest first-week sales totals of the year.
The video won Video of the Year at the 2015 VMAs.
"Band-Aids don't fix bullet holes" became the tagline of the entire 1989 era.
Taylor later said the feud taught her that direct confrontation beats cryptic lyrics.

title: Bad Blood

description: Taylor buries her old selves in a graveyard of easter eggs — the scorched-earth comeback that launched the reputation era.

pops.text: After a year of total silence, this comeback single broke YouTube's 24-hour record with 43.2 million views.
One tombstone reads "Nils Sjöberg" — the fake name she used as a songwriter on Calvin Harris's hit.
"The old Taylor can't come to the phone right now... 'cause she's dead" — the line that launched a thousand memes.
Joseph Kahn directed; the video is stuffed with easter eggs about her feuds and tabloid sagas.
The bathtub full of diamonds references the headlines around the Kim Kardashian robbery-era drama.
A squad of past-Taylors brawl at the end — the 2009 VMAs Taylor, the "Shake It Off" cheerleader, and more.
It debuted at #1, her fifth Hot 100 chart-topper.
The snake imagery reclaimed the snake emoji that trolls had spammed across her socials.
The video ends with the Taylors literally fighting over who gets the last word.

title: Look What You Made Me Do

description: A magic note turns Taylor invisible, and she dances barefoot and unbothered through a Los Angeles hotel, subway platform, and rainy streets.

pops.text: Directed by Joseph Kahn and shot over two freezing nights in Los Angeles.
It premiered during her acceptance speech at the 2018 iHeartRadio Music Awards.
A stranger slips her a sparkling note — when she checks the mirror, her reflection is gone. She's invisible.
Locations include the Millennium Biltmore Hotel, a Metro station, and the Golden Gopher bar.
Free from fame for one night, she dances barefoot through the hotel lobby and into the rain.
Fans compared it to Spike Jonze's Kenzo perfume ad — similar wild hotel dancing (Jonze didn't direct this one).
At the 3:15 mark, a "Joe's Deli" sign nods to then-boyfriend Joe Alwyn.
The second she holds the note up in the bar, everyone turns — she's visible again, and she's smiling.
The song is widely read as being about the fragile early days of her relationship with Alwyn.

title: Delicate

description: A pastel explosion — Taylor and Brendon Urie bicker through a candy-colored dreamscape that secretly hid her next album's title.

pops.text: It shattered YouTube's 24-hour record with 65.2 million views — beating her own "Look What You Made Me Do".
The video opens with a CGI snake bursting into pastel butterflies — reputation is officially dead.
Co-directed by Taylor and Dave Meyers, it's a full 180 from the dark reputation era.
Brendon Urie of Panic! At The Disco duets — and argues — with her through the whole video.
A neon "Lover" sign flashes in the background, revealing the album title months early. Nobody caught it at first.
The opening dialogue secretly hints at the next single, "You Need to Calm Down".
It's a self-love anthem about owning your individuality — "you'll never find another like me".
Her blue dress melting into rainbow streams mirrors her "Delicate" rain dance at the same timestamp.
Rolling Stone called it "campy," "bubbly," and "a totally canonical Taylor lead single".

title: ME!

description: A technicolor trailer-park pride parade packed with celebrity cameos, ending with Taylor and Katy Perry burying their feud in burger-and-fries costumes.

pops.text: An LGBTQ+ anthem that name-checks GLAAD and ends with a call to sign a pro-equality petition.
The video is a technicolor trailer park populated by queer icons and allies.
Cameos include Ellen DeGeneres, RuPaul, Laverne Cox, and the Queer Eye cast.
The finale: Taylor in a burger costume hugs Katy Perry in a fries costume — their years-long feud officially over.
It won Video of the Year at the 2019 VMAs — her second win in the category.
The linked petition gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures for the Equality Act.
"Shade never made anybody less gay" became the summer's defining lyric.
She performed it at the 2019 VMAs surrounded by drag queens.
She later called it the most deliberately political statement she'd made to that point.

title: You Need to Calm Down

description: Taylor transforms into "Tyler," an obnoxious male alter-ego, to show how differently the world treats men and women.

pops.text: Her solo directorial debut — written by, directed by, owned by, and starring Taylor Swift, per the credits.
She plays "Tyler," a manspreading, wall-urinating, yacht-partying caricature of male privilege.
Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson voices Tyler in one scene.
Her dad makes his acting debut as the unimpressed tennis umpire.
A subway wall shows her old album titles as graffiti with a "No Scooters" sign — a jab at Scooter Braun's masters grab.
Another sign reads "Missing: if found, return to Taylor Swift" — also about the masters fight.
Tyler high-fives 19 floating hands — fans read it as her age (19) during the 2009 Kanye VMA moment, and the 19th Amendment.
The video dropped February 27, 2020 — the anniversary of the 19th Amendment's Supreme Court victory.
It ends with Taylor-as-director asking Tyler to be "sexier, more likable" — the note women in Hollywood hear constantly.

title: The Man

description: Taylor climbs inside a glowing piano and drifts through a moss-covered forest and a stormy sea — a lockdown-filmed fairy tale she directed herself.

pops.text: Written, directed, and styled by Taylor — filmed under COVID lockdown with a tiny masked crew.
She did her own hair, makeup, and styling for the entire shoot.
It starts in a candlelit cottage — fans spotted a photo of her grandfather Dean, who fought at Guadalcanal.
She climbs into the piano and lands in a moss-covered forest, playing a piano that sprouts a waterfall.
Next piano-portal: she's clinging to a piano in a churning ocean.
The video is part one of a story — "willow" continues it.
"cardigan" debuted at #1 on the Hot 100 — her sixth chart-topper and second #1 debut.
Cardigan plus folklore made her the only artist ever to debut at #1 on the Hot 100 and Billboard 200 in the same week.
She started selling the actual cardigan from the video on her site the very same day.

title: cardigan

description: Taylor confronts her insecurities head-on: a giant Taylor crashes a dinner party, then she watches her own funeral as her "kids" fight over the will.

pops.text: Written and directed by Taylor — the lead single from Midnights, her tenth studio album.
"It's me, hi, I'm the problem, it's me" — the most quoted lyric of 2022.
A giant Taylor illustrates "I'm a monster on the hill, too big to hang out" — then gets shot with a bow and arrow.
The original cut showed a scale reading "FAT" — she later edited the word out after backlash.
At her own funeral, comedians Mike Birbiglia and John Early play her sons, fighting over the will.
Birbiglia thought he was being catfished when Taylor texted him the offer — he said yes anyway.
The will leaves her beach house to her cats as a sanctuary — and her kids get 13 cents each. Thirteen, obviously.
Daughter-in-law Kimber wears Taylor's actual Fearless-era tour gown.
It spent eight weeks at #1 — her longest-running chart-topper.

title: Anti-Hero
willow
description: A witchy fairy tale that picks up where "cardigan" left off — Taylor follows a golden string through a magic piano into an autumn forest, a glass box, and a moonlit rendezvous.

pops.text: It picks up exactly where "cardigan" ended — Taylor is still drenched from her ocean voyage, sitting in the same cabin.
Her third self-directed video, after "The Man" and "cardigan" — all released within the same year.
The golden string is a direct nod to folklore's "Invisible String": "one single thread of gold tied me to you."
Gold has been her code for Joe Alwyn across three albums — reputation, Lover, and folklore.
The piano opens into a rabbit hole beneath a willow tree's roots in an autumn forest.
She spots her love interest — tour dancer Taeok Lee — reflected in a moonlit pool.
The glass-box scene is fame itself, by her own admission: trapped inside while everyone watches from outside.
Shot by Oscar-nominated cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto, who also filmed "cardigan".
It debuted at #1 on the Hot 100 — her seventh chart-topper and third #1 debut — released as a total surprise with evermore.

title: All Too Well (10 Minute Version)
description: A 15-minute short film — Taylor's directorial debut — starring Sadie Sink and Dylan O'Brien in a devastating autumn romance told in chapters.

pops.text: Written and directed by Taylor herself — her debut as a film director, shot on rich 35mm film.
Sadie Sink was 19 and Dylan O'Brien 30 when cast — the pointed age gap is the whole point.
She told Seth Meyers they were the only two actors she ever imagined — if Sink had said no, there'd be no film.
The film unfolds in chapters like a novel, from honeymoon warmth to a brutal kitchen-table fight.
Eagle-eyed fans spotted a "fuck the patriarchy" keychain — the film's most memed easter egg.
At 10 minutes 13 seconds, it became the longest #1 song in Hot 100 history, dethroning Don McLean's "American Pie".
Taylor appears at the end as the older "Her," watching her younger self from across the years.
It won the Grammy for Best Music Video in 2023 — and screened at both Tribeca and TIFF film festivals.
The song was first written a decade earlier during Speak Now tour rehearsals, then cut down from ten minutes to five.

description: The only official music video Phish ever made — four guys in scuba gear, swimming through an aquarium toward their own New Year's Eve stage.

pops.text: This is it — the only official music video Phish ever produced. Bassist Mike Gordon directed it himself in 1994.
The band spends the clip in scuba gear, diving through a giant aquarium — then surfaces onto the stage of their own 1993 New Year's Eve show, which was aquarium-themed.
The first single from Hoist (1994), the song was Phish's first to chart — it hit #33 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Tracks that summer.
The video got airplay on MTV, and even appeared on Beavis and Butt-Head. The cartoon duo, reportedly, was not impressed.
The lyrics came from real life: Tom Marshall's bout with mononucleosis gave the song its germy title.
Phish first played it at midnight on New Year's Eve 1993 — as a wordless jam melting out of 'Auld Lang Syne.' The full song didn't arrive until April 1994.
Hoist was recorded in late 1993 in Woodland Hills, California with producer Paul Fox — Phish's deliberate, guest-packed bid for a wider audience.
The album features Alison Krauss, Béla Fleck, Tower of Power's horn section, and Star Trek actor Jonathan Frakes on trombone.
To promote Hoist, Gordon also directed Tracking, an experimental short film about the recording sessions.
Live, 'Down with Disease' became a jam vehicle — the longest standalone version, from December 1995, runs over 31 minutes.

title: Down with Disease

description: Phish's 1994 bid for the radio dial — a drunken-seatbelt ballad with cryptic lyrics, captured live at their legendary Clifford Ball festival.

pops.text: The second single from Hoist — Phish's 1994 attempt to make a real, radio-friendly record.
It was cut in late 1993 at the American Recording Company in Woodland Hills, California, with producer Paul Fox.
Trey once summed the song up bluntly: it's about 'sitting in a car with the seatbelt on, drunk.'
The strange lyrics name Elihu and Leemor — characters from a private mythology Trey and Tom Marshall had been building for years.
It peaked at #49 on the Radio & Records rock chart in the summer of 1994 — modest, but proof the band could reach radio.
Rock veterans Little Feat covered it on their 2000 album Chinese Work Songs — one of the highest compliments a jam band can get.
Hoist's guest list reads like a variety show: Alison Krauss, Béla Fleck, Tower of Power's horn section, even Star Trek's Jonathan Frakes.
This clip comes from The Clifford Ball, Phish's 1996 festival on a decommissioned Air Force base in upstate New York — released as a full DVD.
The studio cut is a tidy 4:39; on stage the song usually stays close to that length — a rarity for this band.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall — the duo behind most of Phish's best-known songs.

title: Sample in a Jar

description: A hypnotic vocal round from 1990's Lawn Boy — Phish at their most happily lethargic, bouncing off the studio walls.

pops.text: From Lawn Boy, Phish's second studio album — released in 1990 on a tiny indie label, Absolute A Go Go Records.
Elektra Records reissued Lawn Boy in 1992 after signing the band, giving this homemade recording a major-label afterlife.
The song is built as a vocal round — all four members singing the same melody in a canon, each chasing the last.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it turns a surreal dream — bouncing around an empty room — into a pop song.
One reviewer called the studio take a 'tantalizing outtake from some unreleased sessions' — the band at its most masterfully sleepy.
It's the opening track of A Live One (1995), Phish's live album — captured at the Boston Garden on New Year's Eve 1994.
That live version features trumpets, trombones, and saxes — a one-off brass army for a band that's normally a four-piece.
At about three and a half minutes, it's a short breather in concert — the band rarely stretches it into a jam.
Lawn Boy was where Phish learned to use a studio, setting up the far more polished A Picture of Nectar two years later.
Three decades on, it's still a setlist regular — the rare Phish song you could memorize after one listen.

title: Bouncing Around the Room

description: From a three-minute blast to a forty-minute odyssey — the song that became Phish's greatest jam lottery ticket, shown here at their network-TV debut.

pops.text: You're watching history: Phish's first-ever network television appearance, on the Late Show with David Letterman, December 30, 1994.
The song comes from 1992's A Picture of Nectar — the album that got them signed to Elektra Records.
In the early '90s, this was a quick three-minute blast — played and gone.
Then the band discovered it could be stretched into a jam vehicle, and the song's whole destiny changed.
By 2012 it had become a heavyweight: a version in Mexico clocked in at nearly 40 minutes — the longest 'Chalk Dust' ever.
Fans now treat it like a lottery ticket. You never know whether you'll get the short blast or the epic.
The stop-start riff makes it a perfect launchpad — the band argues musically for a while, then lands back together.
It's been played hundreds of times, and its longest versions rank among the biggest improvisations in Phish history.
The title comes from the lyrics — a narrator who can't shake the chalk dust off everything.
From a three-minute single to a forty-minute odyssey — few songs have evolved quite like this one.

title: Chalk Dust Torture

description: Phish's biggest-ever chart hit (#11 Mainstream Rock) — a tight three-minute pop song from the album where a U2 producer taught a jam band to edit.

pops.text: This is Phish's highest-charting single ever — it climbed to #11 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart.
From Billy Breathes (1996), produced by Steve Lillywhite — the U2 and Peter Gabriel producer who made the band cut their jams and focus on songwriting.
It was first played live at a benefit show in Lowell, Massachusetts, where activist Gloria Steinem introduced the band.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it was recorded at Bearsville Studios near Woodstock, New York, in early 1996.
Many of the album's ideas came from a songwriting trip the two took to the Cayman Islands — they presented the results on a cassette nicknamed 'King Cayman Baluga.'
The sessions started weird: the band first recorded random notes one at a time in an experiment they called 'The Blob,' using vibraphone, Mellotron, and theremin.
Most of 'The Blob' was scrapped — but a couple of minutes survived inside the album's 'Swept Away' and 'Steep.'
The studio version is a tight 3:48 — one of the shortest songs Phish ever recorded.
The album went Gold in 1999 — Phish's best-selling studio record, and a 2018 vinyl reissue was limited to 7,500 copies.
On stage, 'Free' is a different animal — the band stretches it into a full-throated rock anthem far beyond its three-minute frame.

title: Free

description: The hardest-rocking three minutes of Billy Breathes — Phish's 1996 breakthrough, recorded with more discipline than they'd ever shown.

pops.text: Track two on Billy Breathes — the 1996 album where Phish finally learned to make a proper studio record.
It's a lean 3:58 — producer Steve Lillywhite forced the band to chop their sprawling ideas into tight songs.
Lillywhite came from U2, Peter Gabriel, and the Rolling Stones — the band wanted him to make them sound like a real rock band.
Recording happened at Bearsville Studios in upstate New York, during the first half of 1996.
The sessions began with an odd experiment called 'The Blob' — the band recording single notes at random, one turn at a time.
They reached for vibraphones, a Mellotron, and a theremin. Most of it never made the album.
Billy Breathes was released on Elektra Records in October 1996 and went Gold three years later.
Its lead single 'Free' became Phish's biggest chart hit — #11 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart.
'Character Zero' is the album's hardest-rocking moment — a short, sharp burst of guitar muscle between the ballads.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall — the pair behind nearly everything on the record.

title: Character Zero

description: A waltz-time refusal of every career except one — wasting time with you — recorded live at Deer Creek in the summer of '96.

pops.text: This version comes from Deer Creek, Indiana, August 13, 1996 — officially released as part of the Live Phish concert series.
The studio original is track three on Billy Breathes, Phish's 1996 Gold record, running 4:49.
It's a waltz-time ballad built on refusal — the lyrics reject one career after another: actor, writer, painter, farmer, outlaw, climber.
All that rejecting lands on one wish: to waste time with you.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it was recorded at Bearsville Studios with producer Steve Lillywhite.
Trey turned it into a solo staple, playing it dozens of times alone with an acoustic guitar on his own tours.
Fans sing every word — it's one of the rare Phish songs that works better quiet.
Billy Breathes was the band's sixth studio album, released by Elektra in October 1996.
It's stayed in the rotation for decades — Phish were still playing it at Dick's Sporting Goods Park in Colorado in 2021.
For a band famous for twenty-minute jams, 'Waste' proves they could say everything in under five.

title: Waste

description: The quiet title track of Phish's 2000 album — an aurora-inspired hush that grew out of songwriting weekends in Stowe, Vermont.

pops.text: The title track of Phish's 2000 album — a song inspired by the northern lights.
Trey watched an aurora from a solar flare months before writing it, and the song grew from that memory.
It debuted on Late Night with Conan O'Brien in late 1997 — nearly three years before the album existed.
The song grew out of writing retreats: Trey and Tom Marshall rented houses in Stowe, Vermont and disappeared for long songwriting weekends.
Béla Fleck guests on banjo — he'd been orbiting the band since the early '90s.
It's an acoustic-driven hush of a song — Phish at their gentlest, with the farmhouse sitting on a hill in the lyrics.
The album is named for the song — a rare case of Phish letting one quiet tune define a whole record.
Farmhouse marked the end of an era — the band went on hiatus just months after the 2000 tour wrapped.
The same album gave the band its only mainstream pop-radio hit: the next song in this batch, 'Heavy Things.'
Twenty-five years later, it's still the song Phish reaches for when the night needs to breathe.

title: Farmhouse

description: Phish's one fling with mainstream pop radio — performed at their millennium festival in the Everglades while the crowd chanted 'cheesecake' at the cameras.

pops.text: Phish's only mainstream pop-radio hit — it reached #29 on Billboard's Adult Top 40 in 2000.
This clip is from Big Cypress, their millennium festival in the Florida Everglades — some 85,000 fans, broadcast live on ABC.
During the broadcast, Trey got the whole crowd chanting 'cheesecake' — purely to confuse the TV audience at home.
Elektra picked it as the Farmhouse radio single over rockier options — one writer argued 'Bug' would have been the bigger hit.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall, it was first played by a Trey side project in May 1999.
Phish debuted it that September at the Gorge — one fan wrote it 'blew me away: it's poppy, but in a really cool way.'
A critic later called it 'an instant dud, a soft-rock trifle' — but Phish never cared much about radio.
The band played it on Letterman on May 16, 2000 — the day Farmhouse was released.
Trey once pointed out it shares its chords with the Gamehendge epic 'Icculus' — same skeleton, completely different song.
Still the closest Phish ever got to dentist-office radio — and their fans love it anyway.

title: Heavy Things

description: Mike Gordon's slinky cow-funk showpiece from 2014's Fuego — horns, backup singers, and the funkiest groove on a Bob Ezrin-produced record.

pops.text: This is '555' — the slinky cow-funk centerpiece of Phish's 2014 album Fuego, premiered on YouTube before the release.
It was written by bassist Mike Gordon with Scott Murawski of the band Max Creek — one of the few Phish songs not written by Trey.
Fuego was recorded in Nashville in late 2013 with legendary producer Bob Ezrin — the man behind Pink Floyd's The Wall.
The studio version brings in horns and backup singers — a 'nasty horn section,' as one reviewer put it.
The whole album was road-tested first: Phish debuted all of Fuego live on Halloween 2013 in Atlantic City.
That Halloween show was a 'musical costume from the future' — the album didn't come out for eight more months.
Fuego was Phish's twelfth studio album and their first in five years.
One reviewer joked '555' is '555 times better than Winterqueen' — the mellowest song on the record.
Gordon and Murawski have written together for years — '555' is the funkiest thing their partnership ever produced.
Mike usually sings one or two per album — and when it's his song, the groove always wins.

description: The 4:20 opening blast of 2016's Big Boat — debuted at a tour opener in Oregon and still stretching into second-set launchpad territory.

pops.text: The opening blast of Big Boat (2016), produced by rock legend Bob Ezrin.
Phish first played it live on July 21, 2015 — the opening night of summer tour in Bend, Oregon.
It debuted alongside 'No Men In No Man's Land' — both became setlist mainstays within weeks.
The studio version runs exactly 4:20. So does the album's first single, 'Breath and Burning.' The band has never explained the coincidence.
Listen close: Trey yells 'Leo!' right before the piano solo — his on-mic cue to keyboardist Page McConnell.
The studio band is bigger than four: a percussionist sits in — most likely Andres Forero, the drummer from the musical Hamilton.
Forero also played classical percussion on the album's thirteen-minute closing epic, 'Petrichor.'
Big Boat was recorded on the fly — Nashville, Manhattan, Burlington, even the band members' own houses.
A six-song second set in 2015 — 'Blaze On' into 'Twist' into 'Light' — showed how far the song could stretch live.
Written by Trey Anastasio and Tom Marshall — the most prolific songwriting partnership in the band's history.

title: Blaze On
